headline: 2027 Photo Editing Software: Which One is Right for You
alternativeHeadline: 2027 Photo Editing Software: Which One is Right for You | Alan Ranger Photography
description: Compare Lightroom Classic, Lightroom, Luminar, Affinity, DxO, Capture One, ON1, Pixelmator Pro and Photoshop, plus specialist tools, to choose your 2027 editing workflow.
articleBody: Editing guide · 2027 edition Choose an editor that fits the way you photograph The best photo editing software is the one that helps you organise your photographs, make considered adjustments and finish an image with confidence. This guide compares nine main editors and two specialist tools. Start with what you need to do, then choose the software that supports it. Updated 5 November 2026 for photographers planning their 2027 workflow. Features and buying options reflect information available at this update. Where I would start For photographers who want to manage a growing library and develop their RAW files on a computer, Lightroom Classic remains my principal recommendation . Lightroom deserves a separate recommendation for people who prefer editing across devices. They share many editing tools, but the way you store, organise and access photographs differs. Manage a photo library Start with Lightroom Classic. Compare Lightroom if cloud access matters more, or Capture One for a studio workflow. Edit individual images Compare Affinity, Photoshop and Pixelmator Pro for layers, retouching and more detailed image work. Make creative adjustments Consider Luminar or ON1 for accessible effects and assisted editing. Keep control over how far you push the result. You do not need to buy several packages at once. Learn one main editor, establish a reliable backup routine and add a specialist tool only when you can identify a task your current software struggles with. In this guide Quick comparison 1. Photoshop Nik Collection and Topaz Photo How to choose and test Common questions Photo editing software compared for 2027 These are different kinds of tools, so the order is a reading guide rather than a league table. Adobe UK price reference: at this update, Adobe lists the Lightroom 1TB plan at £11.99 a month and the Photography 1TB plan at £19.97 a month, including VAT on annual plans billed monthly. Both include Lightroom and Lightroom Classic; Photography also includes Photoshop. Check Adobe's current plans before subscribing. Nine editors worth considering Choose the workflow first. A photographer delivering hundreds of images needs different strengths from someone making a carefully layered version of a single photograph. 01 · Desktop library and RAW workflow Adobe Lightroom Classic Lightroom Classic brings image organisation and non-destructive RAW development together on your computer. A catalogue records edits and information about files stored on your drives. Keywords, ratings and collections help you find photographs long after the shoot. Its editing tools cover exposure, colour, lens correction and selective adjustments, with AI-assisted masking and noise reduction for supported images. The Print module and external editor workflow are useful when you want to take an image beyond a screen. The main commitment is learning how the catalogue relates to your folders. Back up both the catalogue and the original photographs: one does not replace the other. Classic can sync selected material with Adobe's ecosystem, but it is a different workflow from Lightroom's cloud library. My recommendation: start here if you want a structured desktop workflow and control over a growing archive. Explore Lightroom Classic · Learn Lightroom in Coventry · Learn Lightroom Classic from home with expert one-to-one Zoom tuition 02 · Desktop, mobile and web Adobe Lightroom Lightroom is a distinct application with a simpler interface and a workflow built around access across devices. Its cloud library lets you continue editing on a phone, tablet, computer or web browser, within your plan's storage allowance. It offers substantial RAW and selective editing capabilities. The desktop app can also work with local files, so it is misleading to describe every Lightroom workflow as cloud-only. Decide whether your priority is local browsing or a synced library before importing a large archive. Classic's catalogue structure, printing controls and desktop workflow may suit an established library better. Lightroom is the more natural starting point when convenience across devices matters most. Adobe's feature comparison explains the differences. Choose it if: you regularly move between devices and want your editing workflow to travel with you. Explore Lightroom 03 · Studio sessions and colour control Capture One Pro Capture One Pro deserves consideration when tethered shooting and precise colour adjustments are central to your work. Its Sessions workflow can keep an individual job together, while catalogues support a broader library. Local adjustments, masks and colour tools give you control over how different parts of a photograph are rendered. The practical question is whether its handling of your files and studio process justifies learning a new application. A perpetual desktop licence and subscription options are available. Mobile, collaboration and studio features depend on the package. Check support for your specific camera and connection method before relying on tethering. Choose it if: you photograph in a studio or want a colour-focused RAW workflow built around individual jobs. Compare Capture One options 04 · RAW quality and lens correction DxO PhotoLab DxO PhotoLab focuses on getting a strong starting point from supported RAW files. Its camera and lens modules apply equipment-specific corrections, while DeepPRIME processing tackles noise and detail. Local adjustments let you refine selected areas. It is worth trialling with high ISO images, detailed landscapes and files from lenses that benefit from optical correction. Compare the result at a sensible viewing size as well as at 100%. Fujifilm X-Trans is supported for compatible cameras in the Elite edition. The old blanket exclusion no longer applies. Essential and Elite differ, so check edition requirements and camera support . Its library tools may be sufficient for a smaller workflow; compare them with your archive needs. Choose it if: RAW processing and optical correction matter more to you than complex compositing. Explore DxO PhotoLab 05 · An integrated desktop alternative ON1 Photo RAW ON1 Photo RAW combines browsing, RAW development, layers, effects and AI-assisted tools in one desktop application. It is a useful candidate if you want an alternative workflow without committing to an Adobe subscription. Photo RAW 2027 is available at this update, with a revised RAW engine, masking changes and updated noise reduction. Compare the standard and MAX editions carefully: plug-in use and some additional tools depend on the package. ON1 offers a one-time purchase as well as subscription bundles. Test responsiveness on your own computer, especially when using layers and AI tools on large RAW files. An extensive feature list only helps if the everyday editing process feels comfortable. Choose it if: you want organisation, development and creative effects together, with a purchase option. Explore ON1 Photo RAW 06 · Approachable AI-assisted editing Luminar Luminar is Skylum's AI-powered photo editor, known to many photographers as Luminar Neo. The desktop application is available for macOS and Windows, with mobile and web offerings in the wider product range. Its strengths include quick enhancement, relighting, sky adjustments and portrait tools. Enhance, Relight AI, Sky AI, Skin AI and Portrait Bokeh AI can reduce the manual selections needed for particular adjustments. Desktop RAW support, layers and non-destructive editing also leave room to refine an image beyond a preset. The approachable interface makes it worth considering for newer editors and photographers who enjoy creative treatments. For extensive library management, compare Lightroom Classic; for detailed pixel-level manipulation, compare Photoshop or Affinity. Platform access and cross-device features depend on the licence. Check the current transfer and syncing options rather than assuming desktop, mobile and web have identical tools. Perpetual access also does not mean every future upgrade or online AI service is included indefinitely: some AI access and assets renew separately. Choose it if: you want an accessible editor with assisted tools, while retaining control over the final appearance. Use sky replacement and generated content deliberately, particularly when a photograph is intended as a factual record. 07 · Layers and retouching with a free core app Affinity The current Affinity app brings photo editing, vector design and page layout into one package. The older description of Affinity Photo as a £69.99 purchase no longer reflects the current core offering. Its photo tools include non-destructive RAW development, layers, masks, retouching, HDR merging and batch processing. This makes it a serious option for individual image work and compositions, particularly if you want detailed controls without a core app subscription. The core app is free with a Canva account. Canva's premium AI tools require a qualifying paid plan. Although it includes RAW and batch tools, assess its image handling against your needs rather than assuming it replaces a dedicated Lightroom-style catalogue. Choose it if: you want powerful image editing and retouching tools with a free starting point. Explore the current Affinity app 08 · An option for Apple users Pixelmator Pro Pixelmator Pro is worth considering if you use a Mac or compatible iPad and want image editing, layers, selections and creative tools in an application designed for Apple's platforms. It suits individual photographs, retouching and projects that combine images with graphic elements. It serves a different role from a desktop catalogue used to organise years of shoots. Pixelmator Pro is included in Apple Creator Studio, and the Mac version is also available as a standalone purchase. The iPad offering, feature availability and system requirements need checking against your device and purchase route. Photomator remains a separate product; it should not be confused with Pixelmator Pro. Choose it if: you work on Apple devices and want an alternative for detailed image editing. Explore Pixelmator Pro and buying options 09 · Retouching and compositing Adobe Photoshop Photoshop becomes useful when you need to work deeply on an individual image: combine exposures manually, build a composite, make precise selections or carry out detailed retouching with layers and masks. For many photographers it works alongside a RAW editor. Organise and develop a shoot in Lightroom Classic or Lightroom, then use Photoshop for the images that need more detailed work. It does not provide the same kind of photo catalogue. There is more to learn than most beginners need for everyday exposure and colour adjustments. Begin with a clear task and learn the tools needed to complete it, rather than trying every feature. Choose it if: your editing regularly goes beyond RAW development into detailed retouching or combining image elements. Explore Photoshop · Check Photography plan inclusions Specialist tools: add them for a specific reason DxO Nik Collection Nik Collection is a creative finishing suite for colour, black and white, film-inspired treatments and selective adjustments. Silver Efex is the obvious place to explore monochrome interpretation; Color Efex and Analog Efex offer other ways to shape a finished image. The collection works with compatible host editors and can also run standalone. It is not a replacement for organising and developing an entire RAW archive. Check the current host and file-format requirements for the way you intend to use it. Explore Nik Collection Topaz Photo Topaz Photo concentrates on noise reduction, sharpening, upscaling and image recovery. It is worth testing when a particular file needs help beyond your main editor's tools. Compare it with noise reduction already included in your RAW editor before paying for another package. Inspect fur, feathers, foliage, faces and text carefully: an apparently sharper image can also contain artificial detail. Current Topaz Photo plans are subscription based; check renewal costs and local versus cloud processing inclusions. Explore Topaz Photo My approach: add a specialist tool to solve a recurring problem. Buying another editor is less useful than learning how to make restrained, repeatable adjustments with the software you already have. How to choose your photo editor Make a shortlist of two applications, then edit the same small set of your own photographs in each. Include a high ISO file, difficult highlights, a portrait and a detailed landscape. Test the whole process, from finding the files to exporting the finished photographs. Check compatibility. Confirm your camera's RAW format, operating system, memory and graphics requirements. Decide where originals live. Local drives and cloud libraries need different storage and backup plans. Test everyday adjustments. Crop, set white balance, recover highlights, refine colour and make a local adjustment. Judge the result. Compare at normal viewing size, then inspect for halos, noise and unnatural textures. Check the total commitment. Compare annual cost, renewal prices, major upgrades, cloud storage and time-limited AI services. If you switch software, do not expect all previous edits, masks, collections or plug-in settings to transfer perfectly. Try a small selection first and keep your original files and existing catalogue backed up. What matters for 2027? The useful changes are practical: better assisted selections, more capable noise reduction, additional cross-device workflows and changes to how software is sold. Affinity's free core app, Apple's Pixelmator Pro offering and ON1 Photo RAW 2027 broaden the options. These are available products and current buying models, rather than promises about unreleased features. Keep asking whether a new tool improves your own workflow and whether the edit supports what you wanted the photograph to communicate. Learn a workflow you can repeat Choosing software is the beginning. The next step is knowing what to adjust, why it matters and when to stop. My Lightroom and photo editing course in Coventry helps you build confidence using your own photographs. For individual help from home, book one-to-one editing lessons over Zoom . Bring the images you find difficult and the questions you want to resolve. Photo editing software FAQs What is the best photo editing software for 2027? For a desktop library and RAW workflow, my starting recommendation is Lightroom Classic. Lightroom suits editing across devices; Capture One suits studio work; Affinity and Photoshop suit detailed image editing. The best choice depends on the work you need to do. Are Lightroom and Lightroom Classic the same? No. They share many editing capabilities, but they are separate applications. Classic centres on a desktop catalogue and files on your drives. Lightroom offers cloud access across desktop, mobile and web, with local file editing also available on desktop. Can I edit RAW files without a subscription? Yes. Options include DxO PhotoLab, ON1 Photo RAW and Capture One's perpetual desktop licence. Affinity's core app is free. Check camera compatibility, edition differences and whether major upgrades cost extra. Is Affinity Photo still a paid app? The current unified Affinity app includes free core photo editing tools with a Canva account. Older Affinity Photo licences belong to an earlier product offering. Premium Canva AI features in the current app require a qualifying paid plan. Is Luminar a replacement for Lightroom? It can be an alternative main editor if its RAW and creative tools meet your needs. Photographers who rely heavily on keywording, cataloguing and a large desktop archive should compare its library tools carefully with Lightroom Classic. Do I need Photoshop as well as Lightroom? Not for every photograph. Lightroom can handle much everyday RAW development and selective editing. Photoshop is useful when you need detailed retouching, complex selections or compositing that goes beyond that workflow. Should I buy a separate noise reduction app? Test the noise reduction in your main editor first. A specialist tool such as Topaz Photo may help with particular files, but compare results on your own images before adding another subscription.
